profiled_workloads.selection_reason: Lowest-speedup small case (0.795) and the 1-program launch-bound representative; establishes whether the 13.2us walltime is device- or host-bound.
The one winning large case (1.249) with identical element count and identical logical bytes to timing-7; control that isolates the dtype/math branch from traffic.
Highest-latency large case (83.2us, 0.709) and the bf16 representative of the fp32-upcast regime.
Lowest-speedup workload overall (0.596) and the worst absolute gap; fp32 large case with 2x the logical bytes of timing-3/7.

findings.label: Small cases are host/launch-bound: the device task is 12.6% of the evaluated walltime

evidence.metric: Task Duration(us) mean over 100 measured invocations (_selu_nomask)
Task Duration(us) min / max over 100 invocations
Block Num (programs launched) / aiv_time(us) for fp16 [1024]
mean spacing between consecutive kernel Task Start Time values (109 intervals), i.e. device idle ratio
host node/launch Avg(us) over 110 calls (min 2.32, max 147.90), from api_statistic.csv in the exported vendor report

findings.inference: For selu_-timing-0 the single launched program occupies 1.654us of device time against an authoritative eval walltime of 13.164us, so at most ~13% of the scored latency is the kernel; the remaining ~11.5us is host-side. Consecutive kernel start times inside the op_summary column are 18.34us apart on average while each kernel lasts 1.65us, so the AI vector core is idle ~91% of the collection window. The profiled host node/launch API costs 4.84-5.04us on all four profiled cases and is size-independent, confirming the small cases cannot be improved by touching device code. Caveat that limits how far this can be pushed: the candidate source degrades to the standard Triton launch whenever launcher.enable_msprof_register_tensor is set, so under profiling the direct C launcher is bypassed; the measured host split therefore describes the fallback path and is not a decomposition of the eval path.

findings.label: At identical element count and identical logical bytes, the non-fp16 fp32-math path costs 2.08x the fp16 vector time

evidence.metric: aiv_vec_time(us) / aiv_vec_ratio / Task Duration(us) for fp16 16777216 elements, Block Num 1024
aiv_vec_time(us) / aiv_vec_ratio / Task Duration(us) for bf16 16777216 elements, Block Num 2048
aiv_vec_time(us) / aiv_vec_ratio / Task Duration(us) for fp32 16777216 elements, Block Num 2048
derived aiv_vec_time per 1000 elements, fp16 / bf16 / fp32
derived logical traffic (numel x itemsize x 2) and logical effective throughput at 45.849us fp16 / 83.388us bf16 / 97.083us fp32

findings.inference: timing-3 and timing-7 move the same 67,108,864 logical bytes over the same 16,777,216 elements and launch a pure vector kernel, yet the vector pipe is active 27.21us in the fp16 case and 56.66us in the bf16 case. Per element that is 2.08x. Because bf16 and fp32 run the same fp32 expression while only bf16 pays the bf16->fp32 and fp32->bf16 conversion passes, the fp32 case (2.759 ns/Kelem) is the cleaner estimate of the pure fp32-expression cost and the extra 0.618 ns/Kelem on bf16 (~22% of its vector time) is attributable to the two conversion passes; the remaining ~1.70x over fp16 is the cost of evaluating the curve in fp32 instead of fp16. Decisive scale check: the candidate's vector pipe alone (56.66us) is essentially the entire reference latency for timing-7 (59.03us), and for timing-11 the vector pipe (46.29us) is likewise essentially the reference's 49.30us. So the 1.4-1.7x large-case gap cannot be closed by launch or blocking parameters; it requires reducing per-element vector work. Logical throughput is derived from the frozen spec, not measured physical HBM bytes, and no calibrated bandwidth ceiling was obtained, so no saturation or Roofline claim is made.

findings.label: Scalar prologue cost is purely per-program; the 8192 block cap doubles it on bf16/fp32 without evidence of internal sub-tiling

evidence.metric: derived aiv_scalar_time per program, fp16 / bf16 / fp32

findings.inference: Scalar active time scales with program count, not with element count: 5.8355us at 1024 programs versus 12.4634/12.8398us at 2048 programs, i.e. 5.7-6.3ns per program regardless of dtype or per-program tile size. The block cap of 8192 for the non-fp16 dtypes therefore costs roughly 6.6us of extra scalar work on the 4096x4096 cases. The per-program scalar cost being constant across two different tile sizes (16384 fp16 elements vs 8192 bf16 elements) is evidence against significant multi-buffer-induced internal sub-tiling in the 8192-element programs; small within-program loop overhead would show up as a higher per-program cost at the larger tile. This is medium confidence because internal sub-tiling can only be settled with IR/instruction mapping, which was not collected. Note also that this scalar saving is bounded: halving programs would not touch the vector floor above.

findings.label: fp32 keeps the same per-program tile as fp16 in bytes but spends 3.9x the MTE2 active time of bf16

evidence.metric: aiv_mte2_time(us) / aiv_mte2_ratio / aiv_mte3_time(us) / aiv_mte3_ratio, fp32 2048 programs
aiv_mte2_time(us) / aiv_mte2_ratio / aiv_mte3_time(us) / aiv_mte3_ratio, bf16 2048 programs
aiv_mte2_time(us) / aiv_mte2_ratio / aiv_mte3_time(us) / aiv_mte3_ratio, fp16 1024 programs
derived per-program tile bytes (block x itemsize), fp16 timing-3 / bf16 timing-7 / fp32 timing-11

findings.inference: timing-11 and timing-3 both move 32 KiB per program, and timing-7 moves 16 KiB per program, so fp32's per-transfer size is not smaller than fp16's. Nevertheless fp32's MTE2 pipe is active 27.36us versus 9.45us for bf16 at the same 2048 program count, and versus 7.02us for fp16 at 1024 programs. fp32's logical effective throughput (1.383 TB/s) is close to fp16's (1.464 TB/s) while bf16 sits at 0.805 TB/s, so the fp32 case moves its 2x bytes at nearly the fp16 rate while bf16 is well below both: this is consistent with bf16 being held back by per-element vector conversion cost rather than by transfer, and with fp32 approaching a transfer-related limit. This cannot be promoted to a bandwidth-saturation or bytes-per-MTE2 claim because GM_to_UB/UB_to_GM byte counters, aiv_mte2/aiv_mte3 instruction counts, bank-conflict ratio and any calibrated hardware bandwidth ceiling were not collected in this round.

performance_interpretation: Round 1 (solution 25e45841, geo_mean 0.825, 36/36 PASSED) contains two distinct regimes, so no single bound describes the run. Nine of the twelve timing workloads are 12.2-14.4us calls whose device kernel is only ~1.65-2.2us; they are host/launch-bound and are decided at ~0.79-0.93 by non-device time. Three large workloads are fully device-bound (aiv_time equals task duration to within 0.2%: 44.93/45.85, 83.10/83.39, 97.00/97.08), and there the candidate's own vector pipe is as large as the reference's entire latency (fp16 wins at 45.85us vs 56.93us reference because it uses native fp16 math at 16384-element tiles; bf16 83.39us and fp32 97.08us lose because the fp32-math path costs 1.70-2.08x vector time per element). The single largest waste that the evidence supports removing is therefore the per-element vector work in the non-fp16 branch, not the block size, the program count, or the transfer granularity.

next_experiment.action_description: In the non-fp16 path of _selu_nomask/_selu_masked/_selu_strided, stop evaluating the whole curve in fp32. Keep exp() and the (exp(x)-1) cancellation-sensitive subtraction in fp32, but perform the coefficient multiplies, the branch select and the compare in the input dtype (bf16), so the number of fp32-domain vector instructions per element drops while the accuracy-critical term is unchanged. Do not change BLOCK, grid, the unmasked/masked selection, pointer handling, current-stream reads, or the profiler-compatible size() metadata; do not branch on whether timing or profiling is active.
next_experiment.expected_impact: For selu_-timing-7: aiv_vec_time 56.66us -> ~44us or lower (per-element 3.377 -> <=2.6 ns/Kelem), Task Duration 83.39us -> ~72us, eval speedup 0.709 -> >=0.80, with Block Num unchanged at 2048 so any change is attributable to the vector chain and not to program granularity. Small bf16 cases (timing-4/-5/-6) must stay at or above their current 0.813/0.822/0.926. Not expected to move selu_-timing-11, whose binding term is the fp32 MTE2 plus fp32 vector path; that stays a separate follow-up.
next_experiment.risks_and_rollback: Risk: bf16 precision. The recorded bf16 correctness cases already sit at rel_err 0.032/0.060 (correctness-14/-15), and narrowing the multiplies can push the rtol=0.015 tolerance over the edge. Rollback: keep the current full-fp32 expression behind the dtype branch and revert the change if any of correctness-12..15 or the 36-workload contract fails. Second risk: premature narrowing of the negative branch reintroduces the exp(x)-1 cancellation error near x->0, which is why that term must stay in fp32. No layout, aliasing or in-place semantics change is involved, so rollback is a single-file revert with no re-validation of stride behaviour needed.
success_criteria: Full round evaluation: all 36 workloads PASSED, including the bf16 correctness cases (correctness-12..15) under rtol/atol 0.015.
Headline geo_mean strictly greater than the round-1 baseline 0.825.
selu_-timing-7 speedup >= 0.80 (from 0.709) with its device Task Duration reduced, while Block Num stays 2048 and logical traffic is unchanged.
Re-profiled selu_-timing-7 shows aiv_vec_time per 1000 elements below 2.6 ns (from 3.377), which is the prediction that distinguishes this mechanism from a block-size or launch effect.
No regression on selu_-timing-3 (currently 1.249) and on the three small bf16 cases selu_-timing-4/-5/-6.

warnings: msprof and simulator timing is diagnostic and is not eval latency; the authoritative numbers remain the round-1 eval latency and geo_mean.

Requested MTE2/MTE3 instruction counts, GM_to_UB / UB_to_GM bytes, bytes-per-MTE2 and bank-conflict ratio were NOT obtained. The metrics-level collection produced only a base collection (op_summary/op_statistic/api_statistic/task_time, no Memory.csv or ResourceConflictRatio.csv), and the upgrade to instruction level was cancelled by the service (status RUN_CANCELLED, stage DURING_PROFILE) with an explicit instruction to report only persisted results. Those quantities remain unmeasured for round 1.

The candidate source falls back to the standard Triton launch when launcher.enable_msprof_register_tensor is set, so the direct C launcher used by the eval is bypassed under profiling. The measured host node/launch cost (4.84-5.04us avg, min 2.15-2.37) therefore describes the fallback path and must not be treated as the eval-path host breakdown or subtracted from eval latency.

selu_-timing-11: the profiled device duration (97.083us) exceeds the authoritative eval latency (82.649us) by 17%, while timing-3 and timing-7 agree within 0.3% (45.849 vs 45.588 and 83.388 vs 83.246). Absolute timing-11 device durations are inflated under this collection; only its pipe ratios and relative comparisons are used here.

No reference-side (PyTorch/FlagGems) profile was collected in this round, so 'equal traffic' between candidate and reference for the large cases is an eval-spec assumption, not a measurement; the reference block dims and transfer granularity remain untested.
open_questions: What actually consumes the ~11.5us of non-device time on the 13.2us small cases? The host launch API is measurable only on the fallback path under profiling, so the eval-path split between Python dispatch, CANN launch and harness overhead is still unknown.

Why does selu_-timing-11's profiled device duration exceed its eval latency by 17% while the other large cases match to 0.3%? Its op_summary rows form two clusters (~95-96us and ~99-101us), which is not explained by anything measured here.
Does the bf16/fp32 8192-element program get internally sub-tiled by the compiler to fit UB? The constant per-program scalar cost argues against it, but only IR/instruction mapping can settle it.

What is the actual GM_to_UB/UB_to_GM byte count, MTE2/MTE3 instruction count and bytes-per-MTE2 for these kernels, and what is the calibrated HBM bandwidth ceiling on this 910B4? Without them no bandwidth-saturation statement is possible for the fp32 case.

Could the bf16/fp32 block cap be raised from 8192 to 16384 after reducing fp32 live range? The recorded buffer probes show the current expression needs 2,097,408 bits against 1,572,864 available at 16384 for SELU bf16/fp32, so this is a compile-feasibility question, not a tuning question.
